#7661. U. Colorado Regent-vs.-Regents Lawsuit, Cannabis, Race, and Legislative Immunity

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From James v. Rennison, decided Friday by Judge Philip Brimmer (D. Colo.), plaintiff's allegations:

Regent Wanda James is an elected member of the University of Colorado Board of Regents …. Regent James is the second Black woman to be elected to the Board and is the only Black regent currently on the Board. Regent James is also a prominent Black cannabis owner and was the first Black owner of a cannabis dispensary in the United States. Regent James has used her position on the Board to advocate for communities of color.

In late 2024 and early 2025, the Colorado School of Public Health ("CSPH") developed a public health campaign called Tea on THC. The Tea on THC campaign included use of the following image:

Regent James used her position as a regent and as a private citizen to criticize the Tea on THC campaign, asserting that it invoked racist stereotypes. After Regent James criticized the Tea on THC campaign, the CSPH issued a public statement stating that it regretted any distress caused by the imagery used in the campaign and that it acknowledged its responsibility to reflect cultural awareness and sensitivity. In addition to criticizing the Tea on THC campaign, Regent James spoke publicly about the lack of Black leadership within the University of Colorado….

Approximately a month after Regent James spoke out against the Tea on THC campaign and the lack of Black leadership within the University of Colorado, the Board retained two law firms to evaluate allegations against Regent James. The allegations involved Regent James's speech. On July 2, 2025, the Board met to consider censure and sanctions against Regent James. The Board claimed that Regent James was responsible for CSPH's budget being reduced by 50%, although the budget reduction occurred before Regent James spoke about the Tea on THC campaign. Moreover, on January 31, 2025, the Governor's Office communicated to the legislature that it was seeking full elimination of CSPH's cannabis-related funding. At the July 2, 2025 meeting, by a vote of seven-to-one, the Board voted to censure Regent James under Regent Policy 2.M, finding that she had violated Regent Policy 2.J.1 and Regent Policy 2.J.2, which respectively confer regents with a duty of care and duty of loyalty.

In addition to censuring Regent James, the Board adopted a sanctions resolution. The sanctions resolution removed Regent James from all regent committee assignments, precluded Regent James from any future regent committee assignments, and barred Regent James from attending internal or external University of Colorado events in her official capacity.

Regent James sued the other regents, alleging violation of the First Amendment and race discrimination, but the court held that their actions were protected by absolute legislative immunity:

"The principle that legislators are absolutely immune from liability for their legislative activities has long been recognized in Anglo–American law." … Legislative immunity is "similar in origin and rationale to that accorded Congressmen under the Speech or Debate Clause." …

"Absolute legislative immunity attaches to all actions taken in the sphere of legitimate legislative activity." … Courts have found that board members of educational districts and facilities are entitled to legislative immunity, provided that they are acting in a legislative capacity.

Certain duties of the regents appear to be done in a legislative capacity. Traditionally, legislators have "[t]he authority to pass laws and the power of the purse." The Board of Regents "enact[s] laws for the government of the university," and has "control and direction of all funds of and appropriations to the university." Furthermore, the regents must be elected. Thus, the regents bear similarities to legislators in traditional legislative bodies, such as state legislatures….

"[C]ourts have repeatedly recognized that a legislature voting to censure or discipline one of its own members is a core legislative act," thus falling within … the functional test of legislative immunity…. Defendants sanctioned Regent James for violating the duty of care and duty of loyalty. The sanctions resolution indicates that this was due to, among other things, allegations that Regent James requested that officials in the executive and legislative branches pull funding from the Colorado School of Public Health and shift funding from the Tea on THC campaign to grants for marijuana business owners. If the regents were unable to enforce the Board's internal policies, the adoption of such policies would be meaningless, and the regents would be hindered exercising their duties. For example, the regent's statutory power over the "control and direction of all funds of and appropriations to the university," would be diminished if regents could not enforce internal policies prohibiting a regent from acting contrary to the financial interests of the University of Colorado.

{Legislative immunity does not turn "on the official's motive or intent," so it is irrelevant to the immunity analysis whether defendants actually censured and sanctioned Regent James due to violations of the duties of loyalty and/or care or if that was a pretext to censure and sanction Regent James for discriminatory reasons.} …

Frederick Richard Yarger, Meghan Frei Berglind, and William Daniel Hauptman (Wheeler Trigg O'Donnell LLP) represent defendants.

#7658. Deference, the Insurrection Act, and Statutory History

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I recently wrote about the Ninth Circuit's decision in Newsom v. Trump, which ruled that Trump's federalization of the California National Guard last year, was illegal. Previously I assessed the Supreme Court's ruling in the closely related case of Trump v. Illinois. Today, we have a guest post on these and related issues, by Professor Joshua Braver of the University of Wisconsin. Josh is one of the nation's leading experts on the law regulating domestic use of the armed forces, and my coauthor on two articles about exclusionary zoning (see here and here).

The Volokh Conspiracy and I are pleased to be able to feature his post on this extraordinarily important issue. It is cross-posted with the Just Security site. What follows below is written by Josh Braver, not me (Ilya Somin):

On October 23, in Newsom v. Trump, the Ninth Circuit struck down President Donald Trump's June 2025 federalization of the National Guard in Los Angeles. Although I agree with the result, I disagree with its reasoning on deference. The issue is whether courts should defer to the president, that is, give a president significant leeway in their assessment of the facts on the ground and whether those facts meet the statutory criteria for deploying the military. The Ninth Circuit decided to be, in its words, "highly deferential" in both its decision on Los Angeles and its decision on federalizing the Guard in Portland. That line of reasoning also influenced the Seventh Circuit's decision to give "great deference" in the Chicago case.

In adopting this "highly deferential" standard, the Ninth Circuit claimed to rely on the statutory history of domestic military deployment. But that history actually cuts in the opposite direction, against deference, as I discuss extensively in an article just published in the Emory Law Journal. The significance of that history extends beyond the recent decision in Newsom, which concerned the novel use of a little-known statute, 10 U.S.C. § 12406. The larger question is whether courts should defer to a president when they invoke the Insurrection Act, the main and most fearsome statute for domestic deployment of the military.

Legal commentators had previously recognized these stakes in the last significant decision on these domestic deployments. After the Supreme Court blocked the deployment of the Guard in Chicago last December, some called the decision a "pyrrhic victory;" as Jack Goldsmith put it, the Insurrection Act still "lie[s] in the wings." In Goldsmith's view, the Insurrection Act is "much more robust" than § 12406, and the "power authorized here is astounding," in large part because of the "greater claim to presidential deference" under the Insurrection Act. According to Goldsmith and co-author Bob Bauer, "The president will receive very significant deference from courts in his determination that an Insurrection Act predicate is satisfied." The Ninth Circuit's decision on deference only adds fuel to that blazing fire of deference for the Insurrection Act. That line of reasoning is, however, not well supported by the statutory history of the Insurrection Act.

One of Congress's powers under Article I, Section 8 is to provide for "calling forth" the militia for domestic deployment. The most famous, broadest, and most well-used example of Congress exercising this power is the much-discussed Insurrection Act. But the 2025 deployments in Los Angeles, Portland, and Chicago concerned a heretofore obscure statute, 10 U.S.C. § 12406, which permits federalization of the National Guard in cases of (a) invasion, (b) rebellion, or (c) the president's inability, with the regular forces, to execute the laws of the United States. Newsom v. Trump dealt with the rebellion prong (which Ilya Somin discussed here), while the Supreme Court in Trump v. Illinois addressed the prong involving inability to execute the laws with regular forces.

But there is a specific question of deference. The baseline in statutory interpretation is no deference. Legislatures pass laws and then courts interpret them. When the executive exceeds a statute's authorization as interpreted by the judiciary, courts rule that the action is unlawful. That baseline can be displaced for various reasons. But the most straightforward reason is when the statutory text itself provides for deference, and this was the Ninth Circuit's focus.

Statutes may confer discretion on the president by using subjective terms, such as when a provision turns on what the president "judges," "considers," "deems," "determines," or "finds." For example, in Trump v. Hawaii, the Supreme Court concluded that the statute "exudes deference to the President" because the Immigration and Nationality Act, by its terms, authorizes the president to suspend the entry of aliens whenever he "finds" that their entry would be detrimental to the interests of the United States.  As elaborated in my Emory Law Journal article, the text of the Insurrection Act confers deference in only one of the four conditions for its use, because it sometimes uses the term "considers" and sometimes does not.

In contrast,  there are no subjective discretion-conferring terms in 10 U.S.C. § 12406 that could be construed to confer deference on the president. Both in its recent opinion and in its earlier stay order, the Ninth Circuit acknowledged as much:

"Section 12406 does not include express language making the President the sole judge of whether a required exigency exists. Consequently, if we were considering the text of § 12406 alone, we might conclude that the President's exigency determination is subject to review like certain other factual findings that are preconditions for executive action under a statute."

Nonetheless, the court still decided to be "highly deferential" for two reasons:

"[T]he history of Congress's statutory delegations of its calling forth power and a line of cases interpreting those delegations, beginning with Martin [v. Mott], strongly suggest that our review of the President's determinations in this context is especially deferential."

For the moment, let's leave the court's reliance on Mott to the side, though I will return to it later in the essay. What concerns me here is the Circuit's ostensible reliance on the "history of Congress's statutory delegations." That history, the Ninth Circuit acknowledged, consists largely of the evolution of the Insurrection Act, the principal statute governing domestic military deployments, and the one from which 10 U.S.C. § 12406 descends. For the statutory history of domestic deployments, the court relies solely on the Insurrection Act, but it does not examine that history in much depth. The question is whether those changes in text of the statute over time support deference. They do not.

Statutory History of the Insurrection Act

Today's Insurrection Act has four "triggers," or conditions for domestic deployment. Congress provided express language conferring deference for only one: what I refer to as the judicial-proceedings trigger. There is no deference-conferring language in any of the others.  The statutory history supports this reading of the distribution of deference.  In 1792, the Second Congress rejected deferential language in the first Insurrection Act. Congress would revisit the Insurrection Act two more times: in 1861 and in 1871.  In 1861, it granted deference to the one trigger of judicial proceedings. In 1871, it added two new triggers, but without any deference language.

Let's return to the beginning.  In 1792, Congress considered and rejected deferential language before enacting the first Insurrection Act. The first effort to authorize domestic military deployment came as an amendment to a bill regulating the structure of the state militias. The amendment, passed by the Senate in 1792, authorized the president to call out the militia "as the exigence may, in his opinion, require, to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions." The crucial words were "in his opinion." Because the president's "opinion" modified every trigger for calling out the militia, the amendment would have given the president substantial deference.

The most vehement opponent of the amendment was Representative William Vans Murray, who condemned the legislation because it meant that "the time, the cause, and the place in which the militia were to be called out should be all left to the discretion of one man." This violated the core principle of the Constitution: "a Government of definition, and not of trust and discretion." Murray's objection prevailed. The House rejected the amendment and directed Murray and two other members to prepare a separate bill. The resulting Calling Forth Act contained no comparable language conferring deference on the president in its triggers.

In 1861, Congress added the phrase "in the judgment of the President" to the provision (language that today is phrased "[w]henever the President considers"), but only to the judicial-proceedings trigger, establishing deference in that trigger but nowhere else. That change was understood to settle the controversy over President Lincoln's use of force against the seceding states at the Civil War's outset. By giving him deference, it overturned James Buchanan's argument that the President lacked such authority under the Insurrection Act to fight the Civil War.  When Congress added two new triggers in 1871, it carried no comparable language, leaving the judicial-proceedings trigger as the sole trigger with deference.  The remaining triggers, including "rebellion" and "invasion" which the Ninth Circuit treats as the antecedents for those terms in 10 U.S.C. 12406, had no deference.

Martin v. Mott is a much-discussed 1827 Supreme Court decision interpreting the 1795 Calling Forth Act. The Ninth Circuit read Mott as requiring deference to the president. John Dehn and I, among others, believe this misreads the decision, and the court addresses some of those objections. But my concern here is different: how the statutory history casts Mott in a different light and weakens its force as precedent for interpreting either § 12406 or the Insurrection Act to require deference.

First, Mott interpreted an old version of the Insurrection Act statute, the one from 1795. Congress subsequently amended it extensively, including by adding language conferring deference in 1861 but omitting comparable language when it added new triggers in 1871. § 12406's descends from the amended Insurrection Act, and thus its deference must be read in that light.  Second, two of the triggers in today's Insurrection Act were added only in 1871, decades after Mott was decided. Why should Mott's reasoning extend to them at all?

Finally, Mott addressed the invasion trigger, which is no longer part of the Insurrection Act but is now found in a portion of § 12406 not at issue in Newsom v. Trump. Invasion is one of § 12406's three triggers, alongside rebellion and the inability to execute the laws with regular forces. The Ninth Circuit reasoned that if the invasion trigger requires deference, so too must the other triggers under § 12406. I am skeptical.  But even if the Ninth Circuit is right, that is irrelevant to the Insurrection Act because the invasion trigger is no longer grouped with the other triggers in the Insurrection Act.

The statutory history of the Insurrection Act is extensive, but three developments in 1792, 1861, and 1871 have important implications for deference. Before any court again relies on that history to decide whether, and to what extent, deference is warranted, it must do more than the Ninth Circuit did by merely gesturing at it. It must engage with it. That history, properly understood, casts doubt on granting deference for all but one of the triggers authorizing the president to deploy the military. For the most part, the baseline rule of statutory interpretation remains: Congress has legislated the conditions for domestic deployment, and courts must judge for themselves whether the president has met those conditions without unusual solicitude to a president's views on the matter.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7656. Justice Cody Hiland Publicly Criticizes The President For Nominating Him To District Court Instead of Eighth Circuit

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Apparently, the Arkansas Senators are blocking Judge Lee Rudofsky's nomination because Hiland didn't get the nomination.

We are coming into the endgame for President Trump's judicial nominees. Since the election, it seems the President has made (at least) two nominations to the federal bench in Texas: Justice James Sullivan of the Texas Supreme Court for the WDTX seat in Austin and OLC Head Elliot Gaiser for the NDTX seat in Dallas. I say "seems" because the President has not posted these nominations to Truth Social, as that makes it official. But the Senate Judiciary Committee has received questionnaires for both candidates. I have known both of these sharp legal minds for some time, and would welcome their addition to the bench. Will Sullivan and Gaiser get votes? I sure hope so. Over the next six weeks, Republican Senators will need to be motived to vote, while Democrat Senators will pull out every stop to leave these seats open. Plus, there is an entire line of other nominees who are still waiting for votes.

Beyond the district court nominees, there is the question of circuit court nominees. Judge Anna St. John's nomination to the Fifth Circuit and Judge Daniel Domenico's nomination to the Tenth Circuit are pending. They had their hearings some time ago, and should get through. Todd Butler has not even had his hearing yet, so he is down the pecking order. Then there is Judge Lee Rudofksy, a nominee to the Eighth Circuit, who had his hearing back in September. Yet, both of the Arkansas Senators are blocking Rudofsky's nomination. Why? They prefer Justice Cody Hiland, a member of the Arkansas Supreme Court.

There's a problem with Hiland. He has demonstrated absolutely terrible judgment which should permanently disqualify him from holding any public office.

In August, he decided to disclose to a room full of law students private communications between him and the White House Counsel. Worse, rather than teaching students about the value of grace, he promoted belligerence and vindictiveness. In short, the White House approached Hiland about a nomination to the Eighth Circuit. After the vetting process, the White House changed course, and offered Hiland a seat on the federal district court. Hiland refused, and told the White House Counsel to tell President Trump about it. He said all of this on a livestream. You can watch it here, starting around the 16:45 mark:

And I've transcribed the comments for those who prefer to read:

The second thing I want to talk about is you're going to have to learn to be resilient, and maybe this far in your career, maybe it's been easy for you. I don't know, but you're going to have to learn how to be knocked down and then get back up, and then also not to be intimidated. Resiliency is something that is going to carry with you the rest of your career. Now, I'm going to tell you a story that just happened to me because resilience matters even at this point in a career. So, you you want to hear a backstory on something? Nobody ever gets to hear backstories. I'm going to give you a backstory. So, about two months ago, I was contacted about being appointed by the president to the Eighth Circuit. Okay, I had senators who asked me to do it. Applied, went to the interview in front of a White House panel of eight Ivy League attorneys, did an interview, and then got a call. And the call said, "You know what? We're going to recommend that the president appoints you to the Eighth Circuit, and so they started a background check. The FBI goes out, and if you've ever served in these capacities, you know that there's a full field investigation that takes place. And select 12 or 13 agents just investigate you for about six weeks. And in this case, they ask them to finish it in two weeks because they wanted to get it done, and so the FBI went out and they talked to over 130 people about me and my life. And when Dean Crawford is talking about social media, you know that sort of thing matters, okay? Because they go back to the time that you're 18 and they talk to everybody you've ever leased from. They tell you they're going to talk to your girlfriends and everybody else. It's like taking a bath with a brillo pad. Okay, good decisions matter as you go along this course, and so it rocked along. And last Tuesday, I had a meeting. Last Wednesday, I had a meeting for three hours with the Department of Justice, finalizing my Senate Judiciary Committee questionnaire, and it was going to be sent in. And I was told to go home and to expect a phone call from the President of the United States, and to be offered the position. And so I went home and I charged my phone and I called my wife and I said, "You need to come home tonight's the night. We've been through two months of unbelievable minutia of a life that's quite frankly not that interesting. Okay, but I had to have it all, and we had prepared it. It was ready to it was ready to go. And I get a phone call from 202. For those of you don't know, that's Washington D.C. And the man on the other end of the line was not the president of the United States. It was White House Counsel, who, by the way, had recommended that we be chosen. And White House Counsel said the president would like to know if you would be interested in a federal district court position. Eastern District of Arkansas, and I said, "You mean Circuit, Eighth Circuit? No, no, no. Federal District Judge in the Eastern District of Arkansas." And so your mind starts going, "What in the world has happened? What am I hearing?" And so, being belligerent, and at times I said no. That is not a position that I'm interested in. And he came back with after a five second delay of you know not believing what I just said. He said, "So you want me to go back into the Oval Office and tell the President of the United States that you're rejecting an opportunity to be appointed to the federal bench, and I said, "Yes, that's exactly what I want you to tell the president of the United States." And so, you know, I tell that story to say this because I want to be honest. Because too many elected officials are just not transparent, and that happened to me last week. You know what? It's okay because I'd never dreamed of being on the Eighth Circuit. It had never been had come to my mind. But we had an expectation based on an FBI investigation, based on communication from those that make these decisions that it was done. And sometimes, guys, it's not done. Sometimes your expectations are not met. When you're a student here with these kind of people, this kind of quality, not everybody is going to make the top paper. Not everybody is going to make law review. Despite what your expectations may be there are times where your expectations are not going to be met, and it's going to happen for the rest of your life at times. And so, as you begin this career, start developing that resiliency.

Talking to law students is my profession. I can't imagine a judge making such a huge blunder. What lesson are these students taking away here? That you should be so stubborn about getting one position that you refuse another lifetime commission? That you should reveal private communications with the White House in which you admit you were "belligerent"? He is comparing not getting an Eighth Circuit appointment to not getting on law review? No wonder the White House didn't pick him. In my view, making a bad nomination is worse than making no nomination at all (see Butler).  The Eighth Circuit is at a turning point. Judge Stras writes far too many dissents. One more vote could flip the circuit. Arkansas is but one state in the circuit. This stubbornness will spite the good people of those states.

Here's the bottom line. Senators pick Judges who are their friends. Those are the worst possible reasons to pick a judge. We need to reward the people who advance the rule of law, not those who are chummy with Senators. And yes, this applies to Todd Butler too. The Junior Senator from Mississippi told people to choose a different protein. Well, they should have chosen a different judge. But here we are.

Before Texas state Sen. Nathan Johnson, D-Dallas, unleashed a “blue spirit bomb” on opponent Mayes Middleton on Tuesday night in the midterm elections for the Texas attorney general spot, the Thompson Coburn lawyer composed musical scores for Dragon Ball Z, a Japanese anime series about martial artists who defend the world from destruction.

Johnson, who got at least 52% of the vote and is a Dallas lawyer, will be the first Democrat to serve as the Texas attorney general in more than 30 years, Chron.com reports.

The show introduced various terms to the United States, including “Super Saiyan,” which means getting a huge surge of physical strength and hair that stands straight up, and “blue spirit bomb,” which is something released on opponents during an attack.

A piano player, Johnson learned how to write music while working as a lawyer and liked it so much that he decided to quit his job and focus on doing film and television composition, according to the article.

Johnson eventually went back to law and started a solo practice. While looking for office space, he met a landlord connected to a Texas company that licensed the English version of Dragon Ball Z in the United States. The company then hired Johnson in the early 2000s, according to Chron.com.

“It gave me a creative outlet and a cultural connection that very few people have had the opportunity to have,” Johnson said in an interview, according to Variety.

#7653. The Butler Didn't Do It

Todd Butler's bare Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire.

Todd Butler has now posted his questionnaire for the Senate Judiciary Committee. Here is the chronology Butler offers for his nomination:

On June 29, 2026, Senator Roger Wicker contacted me about a potential vacancy on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. I spoke with Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith the following day. On July 1, 2026, an official from the White House Counsel's Office contacted me to arrange an interview. On July 13, 2026, I interviewed with officials from the White House Counsel's Office. Following my interview, I received periodic updates from Senator Wicker about the process. On October I, 2026, President Trump called to inform me that he planned to nominate me for a position on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

There is a very relevant date missing here. On September 28, 2026, Judge Southwick publicly announced that he would take senior status. Yet three months earlier, Senator Wicker contacted Butler about the potential vacancy.

As I said from the outset, the fix was in. There was some sort of deal involving Wicker, Southwick, and the White House. I'm sure this interview was pro forma. and doubt any other candidates were interviewed. Judge Southwick could have announced his intentions at any time in August or early September, but he waited until the last possible moment to jam up the process, and ensure Butler would not go down. I do hope at least one Senator asks Butler if he is aware of any communications in which Judge Southwick, directly or indirectly, conditioned his willingness to take senior status if Butler is the nominee.

As for the rest of the SJQ, let's just say Butler's pantry is bare. Or, the Butler didn't do it.

Butler went to law school between 2005 and 2008, but he wasn't a member of the Federalist Society. That makes sense, as he wrote critically of Justice Scalia, originalism, and the Second Amendment. He wasn't a member while he clerked. Indeed, he didn't become a member of the Federalist Society until 2016. I suspect lots of people joined before or after Trump's victory. It would help with career prospects. He has never held any leadership positions in FedSoc. But rest assured that he was active in the Inn of Court and the Mississippi Bar, holding several leadership positions.

Butler has extensive experience in employment law. In addition to the publications I flagged, Butler speaks and writes often about the EEOC, FLSA, and related topics of municipal law. His only professional exposure to constitutional law involves defendant local officials who are sued for violating First Amendment rights. After Olivier v. City of Brandon, his most significant case was as defense counsel in a wrongful death case. He taught at the Mississippi College of Law "periodic[ally]" between 2008 and 2016 but does not recall which semesters he taught. He also does not have copies of the syllabi.

Here is how Butler describes his pro bono work:

Over the course of my career, I have accepted pro bono clients, typically through the Mission First Legal Aid Clinic or the Mississippi Volunteers Lawyers Project. I have assisted with adoptions, child visitation matters, and other domestic issues. I also have provided pro bono services to a local church, including contract review and procedure drafting, in connection with the operation of a faith-based children's center. I advised a local pastor on a land acquisition that he is considering using for a fellowship facility. And I have volunteered, along with others at my law firm, at Stewpot Community Services, where we served meals to people experiencing homelessness.

There is no pro bono work that would remotely be associated with the conservative legal movement. And no, working for a church does not necessarily make a person conservative.

If I were to show you this questionnaire, without any knowledge of Mississippi politics, would you possibly think this was a viable record for the Fifth Circuit? No.

#7651. New Mexico Supreme Court permanently disbars prosecutor after disciplinary findings

The New Mexico Supreme Court, after hearing from a disciplinary board, has permanently disbarred a prosecutor who was found to have pattern of misconduct that denied defendants fair trials. (Image from Shutterstock)

The New Mexico Supreme Court, after hearing from a disciplinary board, has permanently disbarred a prosecutor who was found to have pattern of misconduct that denied defendants fair trials.

Cosme Ripol, a prosecutor from the district attorney’s office for the Eighth Judicial District in Taos, New Mexico, was disbarred Monday, effective immediately.

All five justices on the state supreme court agreed on the disciplinary board’s recommendation. The proceedings focused on three criminal cases that Ripol prosecuted between 2022 and 2024.

According to coverage by the Santa Fe New Mexican, a pivotal case in the investigation was State v. Desiree Lensegrav, where the defendant was convicted in 2022 of first-degree murder, kidnapping, conspiracy and tampering with evidence.

The New Mexico Supreme Court vacated Lensegrav’s convictions after it learned that Ripol, who had been licensed to practice law in the state since 1986, used inadmissible evidence and made derogatory statements about the defendant during the trial.

“As the supreme court noted, prosecutors are held to a higher standard because of their unique responsibility to seek justice,” said Marcus Montoya, the district attorney for the Eighth Judicial District, in a statement Monday. “When improper tactics are employed in the courtroom, even by an attorney with more than 30 years of criminal law experience, that standard is not met.”

The FBI and Department of Commerce are investigating the case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs secured the extradition of Suvorov with the assistance of the Swedish Authorities.

#7649. S. Ct. Suspends District Court's Injunction Blocking Border Barrier Building

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"There is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim."

From today's Supreme Court unsigned opinion in Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church (with Justice Jackson essentially dissenting):

Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) grants the Secretary of Homeland Security broad authority to construct border barriers and roads "to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States." The same section expressly authorizes the Secretary "'to waive all legal requirements'" as "'necessary to ensure expeditious construction'" of those barriers and roads, and sharply limits judicial review of all claims arising from such waiver determinations. Specifically, the statute provides that "'[a] cause of action or claim may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States'" and courts "'shall not have jurisdiction'" over nonconstitutional claims. §102(c)(2)(A).

Earlier this year, the Secretary invoked Section 102's waiver authority to initiate a border-construction project at the U.S.–Mexico border, in a region that U.S. Customs and Border Protection has designated the "Big Bend Sector." The Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector "is an area of high illegal entry" requiring additional border barriers, and waived the application of a variety of environmental and conservation laws to facilitate expeditious construction.

Shortly thereafter, respondents—an individual river guide, an environmental nonprofit, and a nonprofit organization dedicated to preserving a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas—challenged those waiver determinations by filing suit in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas. Respondents claimed, among other things, that the Secretary's waiver determinations "violat[ed] the major questions doctrine under the U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 1." Although styled as constitutional, that claim simply alleged that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority in issuing the waivers.

On October 2, 2026, the District Court entered a preliminary injunction blocking the Secretary's waivers and halting all associated construction. The District Court acknowledged that its jurisdiction was limited to constitutional claims. But it nonetheless concluded that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" qualified because, in its view, the "major questions doctrine is a constitutional clear statement rule grounded in separation of powers." The court further held that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" was likely to succeed on the merits because the Secretary lacked "'clear congressional authorization' to issue" the waivers. Because the Fifth Circuit lacks jurisdiction to hear this case, IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(C), the Solicitor General filed an application requesting either summary reversal or a stay of the District Court's preliminary injunction.

We grant the requested stay. The Government is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument that the District Court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate respondents' so-called major-questions-doctrine claim. However it is labeled, respondents' claim does not "'alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the United States,'" the only type of claim the statute permits district courts to adjudicate. IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(A). It alleges instead that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority. And we have long recognized that "claims simply alleging" that the Executive Branch has exceeded its "statutory authority are not 'constitutional' claims." Dalton v. Specter (1994).

That conclusion does not change where, as here, a plaintiff invokes the major-questions doctrine. Many canons and rules of statutory interpretation reflect constitutional principles, including "constitutional avoidance, the clear-statement federalism rules, and the presumption against retroactivity." When courts invoke those canons, however, they do so in service of adjudicating statutory claims, not constitutional ones. The same is true when a court invokes "the major questions canon of statutory interpretation." There is no such thing as a "constitutional" major-questions claim….

Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area. But Congress's enactment of IIRIRA §102(c)—which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws—reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert. And courts "of equity cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute." The Government's interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents….

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7647. A World of Independent Nations

Introduction

It is a great pleasure to be here in Jerusalem, and it is especially fitting to discuss “A World of Independent Nations” here in Israel. If any nation understands the importance of sovereignty, national survival, secure borders, and the sometimes inconvenient necessity of putting its own people first, it is Israel.

I come here as an American conservative, as someone who has spent much of his career working on Europe, and I should probably confess at the outset, as an unreconstructed Euroskeptic. I realize that admitting you are a Euroskeptic at NatCon is not exactly an act of great personal courage. It is rather like announcing at Heritage that you have reservations about socialism or Islamism.

But I want to make a broader argument today.

National sovereignty and transatlantic cooperation are not opposites. They are not even in tension. Properly understood, national sovereignty is the basis for meaningful transatlantic cooperation.

For far too long, the foreign policy establishment on both sides of the Atlantic has presented us with a false choice. Either you believe in an ever more integrated West, governed by international institutions and supranational bureaucracies, or you retreat into isolationism. Either Brussels runs Europe, or Europe falls apart. Either Washington manages its allies, or America abandons them.

I reject that choice. There is another model. It is a world of sovereign nations that know who they are, control their own borders, govern themselves, defend themselves, and cooperate when their interests and values coincide—in other words, exactly the sort of international order conservatives should be trying to build.

The Nation-State Is Not the Problem

For the past several decades, nationalism has been treated in much of polite Western society almost as a pathology. Europe in particular was told that its terrible 20th-century history proved that the nation-state itself had failed.

The answer was integration. Then, more integration. Then, when integration produced problems, the answer was invariably still more integration. It reminds me a little of the old joke about socialism: The reason it has never worked is apparently because nobody has ever tried quite enough of it.

The European project originally presented itself as cooperation among sovereign countries. But over time, political authority moved steadily away from national governments and toward institutions increasingly removed from national electorates. As I argued in “U.S. First Principles vs. European Bureaucratic Overreach,” the European Union has increasingly transferred authority away from sovereign nations and into distant institutions with limited democratic accountability.[REF]

This matters because democracy requires a Demos. Someone has to be able to answer the simplest political question there is: Who governs? And if you dislike the answer: How do you get rid of them?

That is easy to understand in a nation-state. It becomes considerably less clear when authority is dispersed among commissioners, courts, councils, agencies, treaties, and qualified-majority voting. It is difficult enough getting rid of a bad congressman. Try voting out the European Commission.

Europe Is Not the European Union

This leads to a distinction that American policymakers repeatedly fail to make: Europe is not the European Union. Europe is a civilization. Europe is a collection of ancient nations. Europe is Britain and France, Poland and Hungary, Italy and Greece, the Baltic States and the Nordic countries, and many others, each with its own history, traditions, loyalties, interests, and democratic institutions. The European Union is an institution.

The two are not synonymous. In fact, one of the most damaging habits in American foreign policy has been to confuse support for Europe with support for European integration. An America First foreign policy should stop doing that.

As I argued recently after Iceland rejected renewed EU accession talks in “Iceland Puts the Freeze on Brussels’ ‘Ever Closer Union,’” Washington should deal with Europe as it actually exists: as a continent of nations. America benefits when democratic allies control their own resources and interests and cooperate voluntarily, including through NATO.[REF]

That is not anti-European. It is profoundly pro-European. It says that the Czech Republic belongs to the Czechs. Poland belongs to the Poles. Hungary belongs to the Hungarians. Britain belongs to the British. And the United States belongs to Americans.

Perhaps this is considered radical these days. I prefer to call it self-government.

America First Does Not Mean America Alone

This brings me to America First.

America First is sometimes caricatured, particularly in Europe, as a doctrine of withdrawal. I think that completely misunderstands it. America First does not mean America alone. It means that American foreign policy should advance American interests.

And we should expect our friends to do exactly the same thing for their countries. America does not want European governments that obediently ask Washington what to do. America wants strong allies. America wants European countries capable of securing their borders, growing their economies, and defending their territory. America wants European NATO members capable of bearing a much larger share of the burden of defending Europe. America wants allies, not dependencies.

That is why sovereignty actually strengthens transatlanticism. America does not ultimately form alliances with regulatory systems. It forms alliances with nations capable of making decisions and honoring commitments.

A weak country that has surrendered responsibility for vital decisions is not made stronger merely because it sits inside a larger bureaucracy. A self-confident nation that can defend itself, control its territory, and act politically is a much more useful ally.

Where Conservatives Must Cooperate

But this cannot mean conservatives retreating behind their own borders and ignoring one another. Quite the opposite: Each nation must decide questions of free speech, border control, family, faith, energy, economic freedom, and defense for itself—but those debates increasingly reach across the Atlantic.

We should be candid. President Trump’s style can sometimes unsettle even our European conservative friends who agree with him on borders, sovereignty, and burden-sharing. That is no reason to abandon cooperation. European conservatives need not become Trumpists. Friends can disagree over tactics, trade, Ukraine, or NATO and still work together where their interests and principles coincide.

So, what should cooperation look like? It should begin with permanent working relationships among think tanks, lawmakers, legal groups, and campaigners. It should be built around particular battles, not a single manifesto. We can cooperate on free speech without agreeing on every foreign policy question.

And it should connect sovereign actors directly: Congress with national parliaments, attorneys general with legal advocates, and governments with governments—not everything mediated through Brussels.

The agenda is clear: speech, borders, family, faith, energy, economic freedom, and defense.

The test is simple. Cooperation should make each nation more capable of governing itself, not less.

A Practical Framework: A Transatlantic Conservative Compact

I propose a Transatlantic Conservative Compact. Not a treaty. Not a bureaucracy. And certainly not a conservative Brussels.

It would be a voluntary network linking conservative governments, lawmakers, think tanks, and legal groups around specific projects. Small working groups could share model laws, legal briefs, and campaign lessons on speech, borders, family, energy, and defense. Members could join one project and decline another.

That is the model. Not uniformity: cooperation.

Free speech is the obvious place to begin because rules written in Brussels or London can govern American platforms and affect what American users see.

The EU’s Digital Services Act can fine the largest platforms according to global turnover.[REF] In 2024, EU Commissioner Thierry Breton even warned Elon Musk before his interview with Donald Trump—an American political event.[REF] Britain’s Online Safety Act can likewise reach services based abroad and impose enormous fines.[REF] Faced with that risk, platforms will often censor first and ask questions later.

American and European conservatives should expose these demands, challenge them in court, and defend clear legal protections for political and religious speech. Alliance Defending Freedom, among others, is doing stellar work in this area.

In “European Democracy Shield: A Threat to Free Speech and Democratic Accountability,” I argued that American and European conservatives need to work more closely together to protect freedom of speech and conscience.[REF]

Border control and mass migration are another such issue. Individual nations must decide whom they admit, who is entitled to remain, and what obligations newcomers owe to the society receiving them. That responsibility cannot simply be outsourced upward.

Borders are not an embarrassing leftover from an unenlightened past. They mark the territory within which democratic government operates. If a government cannot determine who enters its country or effectively enforce its immigration law, we should ask in what meaningful sense it remains sovereign.

Here, American and European conservatives have a great deal to learn from each other. The objective should not be identical policies imposed from above. It should be the exchange of ideas among sovereign governments pursuing the interests of their own citizens.

That also means confronting Islamification directly. Religious liberty must be protected, but political Islam and parallel societies must not be tolerated. Newcomers who wish to live in Western nations must accept our laws, our civic order, and our civilizational inheritance. They need to integrate—or leave.

A Transatlantic Conservative Compact would also involve working together on issues like energy security, economic freedom, family policy, religious liberty, and the defense of Western civilization—and, of course, defense.

The transatlantic alliance remains important, but NATO should be an alliance of sovereign countries accepting reciprocal obligations, not a mechanism for permanently transferring responsibility for European security to the American taxpayer. If European nations are sovereign, then sovereignty comes with responsibilities. One of them is paying for your own defense.

I suspect even my European friends will concede that this particular American enthusiasm for national sovereignty is unlikely to disappear.

Europe Beyond the EU

At Heritage’s Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom, this is increasingly becoming a central part of our work.

Heritage is organizing a major event in Washington called “Europe Beyond the EU.” Its starting point is deliberately provocative: What if the future of Europe is not deeper integration? What if the real intellectual challenge is to imagine European cooperation after the age of centralization? In this tenth-anniversary year of the Brexit referendum, our December 8, 2026, conference will open that conversation, exploring what a European order rooted in sovereign nation-states might look like and how American conservatives can support it.

And we intend to go much further. Our planned Transatlantic Sovereignty Initiative will develop practical alternatives to centralized control over democracy, speech, trade, energy, economic policy, borders, and security. The purpose is not simply to criticize Brussels. It is to develop a positive conservative architecture for cooperation among self-governing nations.

That distinction matters. Euroskepticism cannot simply mean saying “No.” Eventually, we have to explain what we are saying “Yes” to. The answer is a flexible Europe.

  • NATO for collective defense.
  • Bilateral and multilateral agreements where they make sense.
  • Trade among free nations.
  • Voluntary arrangements on security and migration.
  • Cooperation without political absorption.
  • Partnership without permanent centralization.

I have called this elsewhere a functional Europe: sovereign nations using the institution appropriate to the task rather than assuming every problem requires transferring yet another power upward.[REF] That principle works beyond Europe as well.

Conservative Solidarity Without Conservative Globalism

There is, however, a trap here for our own movement. Conservatives rightly criticize globalism. We should therefore be rather careful not to invent a conservative globalism of our own. Our purpose cannot be to replace one transnational ideological establishment with another.

A Hungarian conservative will naturally put Hungary first. A Polish conservative should put Poland first. An Israeli conservative should—and most definitely does—put Israel first. And I make no apology for saying that an American conservative should put America first.

The miracle is not that our interests will always be identical. They won’t. The opportunity is that sovereign nations which possess civilizational confidence can nevertheless recognize enormous areas of common interest.

We can defend the freedom to speak.

We can defend religious liberty.

We can defend the family.

We can secure our borders.

We can resist unelected bureaucracies claiming powers voters never willingly surrendered.

We can defend the inheritance of Western civilization without demanding that every Western nation become politically identical.

And we can maintain a strong Atlantic alliance without asking either Americans or Europeans to surrender their independence.

That is my idea of transatlantic conservative solidarity. Not bland uniformity: solidarity. Not supranational government: cooperation. Not a homogenized West administered from Washington, Brussels, Davos, or anywhere else: a West of free nations.

Conclusion

For most of my professional life, the dominant assumption has been that history was moving relentlessly away from the nation-state. National loyalties were supposedly becoming obsolete. Borders would matter less. Supranational institutions would inevitably become stronger. Politics would become increasingly managerial. And ordinary voters would eventually learn to accept all of this.

I am increasingly convinced that precisely the opposite is happening. The nation has returned because it never really went away.

People want government close enough to control. They want borders that mean something. They want political leaders who are accountable to them. They want to preserve what makes their country their country. And they are increasingly impatient with institutions that tell them these desires are somehow illegitimate.

This is not a crisis for democracy. It is democracy reasserting itself. The challenge for conservatives is to turn that democratic revolt into a durable political order.

A world of independent nations need not be a world of isolation. It can be a world of vigorous cooperation precisely because that cooperation is voluntary.

A confident America should want confident allies. A sovereign Europe can be a better American partner than an increasingly centralized European Union. And nations secure in their own identity are better able to cooperate because they do not fear that cooperation requires their disappearance.

So my argument today is ultimately very simple: Sovereignty is not the enemy of Western unity. It is the foundation of it.

The future of transatlanticism should not be ever closer union. It should be ever stronger nations: independent, democratic, self-confident, able to disagree, able to cooperate, able to defend themselves, and willing, when our principles and interests align, to stand together.

That is the transatlantic alliance worth defending, and that is a world of independent nations worth building.

Paul McCarthy is Senior Research Fellow for European Affairs in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation. This lecture is adapted from remarks delivered at NatCon Jerusalem on October 8, 2026.

#7646. Poe, the Pandemic and a Halloween Lesson for Catholics and Protestants

For many years, I kept a private rule as some men keep a flask in their coat pocket: one novel always at hand, open somewhere, patient, no matter how the briefs and research and obligations piled up.

Lately, I have broken the rule. I’ve felt its absence the way the tongue keeps returning to the place where a tooth once was. Then, the other afternoon, a television appearance was abruptly canceled, and I found myself holding two unclaimed hours like dollar bills found on the sidewalk. The day was bright and sunny, but it was October all the same. The light had that thin, cidery quality, and the shadows lay longer on the lawn than the clock said they had any right to.

It is, as friends of mine insist, Kirktober. Russell Kirk, the sage of Mecosta, Mich., whose “The Conservative Mind” gave postwar conservatism both its pedigree and its conscience, was born in October, and he loved nothing better than a ghost story told by firelight at Piety Hill, his ancestral house. He wrote them too, and wrote them well, for he believed the uncanny was a moral instrument: it reminds us that the universe keeps rules we did not write.

So, in his honor, I wandered from my usual shelves, took down an old leatherbound Poe whose spine had gone soft as a glove, and let it fall open where it wished. It chose “The Masque of the Red Death.”

>>> Manhattan’s Lost Its Screen Presence

The story is hardly longer than a sermon, and it haunted me in a way Poe could not have intended, because the plague years (yes, I mean COVID are not far behind us. His pestilence is “fatal” and “hideous.” “Blood was its Avatar and its seal—the redness and the horror of blood.” The whole business, from first dizziness to last breath, took half an hour.

And then there is Prince Prospero, whose very name is a boast of good fortune and an echo of Shakespeare’s magician, the one who withdrew to an island and commanded the weather. Poe’s prince gathers a thousand of his gayest knights and dames and retires “to the deep seclusion of one of his castellated abbeys.” The courtiers weld the bolts shut behind them. The external world could take care of itself.

One remembers the photographs from our own season of quarantine: the governors at the fine restaurants, the masks lowered for the cameras of the important, the rules that fell on ordinary people like rain and somehow never dampened those who made them.

Inside the abbey, Poe builds a fever dream. There are seven rooms, each a single color: blue, purple, green, orange, white, violet. The seventh is hung in black velvet, and its windows are scarlet, the deep color of blood. No lamp burns in any chamber; instead, braziers on tripods stand outside the tinted glass, throwing firelight through the panes so that every room swims in its own unnatural hue.

Here the masquerade whirls on. The costumes have much of the beautiful, much of the wanton, much of the bizarre, something of the terrible. A mask is a small lie that promises a large one: that you may become anyone, and so nothing can find you. But in the black room stands a great ebony clock, and on each hour it sounds a note so strange that the orchestra falters, the waltzers freeze, the giddiest go pale. The clock is the one guest who cannot be bribed. The rooms run east to west, dawn to dusk, and everyone knows where the last one leads.

At midnight, an intruder appears: 

The figure was tall and gaunt, and shrouded from head to foot in the habiliments of the grave. The mask which concealed the visage was made so nearly to resemble the countenance of a stiffened corpse that the closest scrutiny must have had difficulty in detecting the cheat. 

Prospero, furious at the insult, chases the figure through all seven rooms with a drawn dagger. In the black chamber, the stranger turns, the dagger drops, and the prince falls dead upon the sable carpet. The revelers seize the masker and find beneath the shroud and the corpse-like mask nothing at all, the garments “untenanted by any tangible form.” The Red Death has come and gone.

Poe knew this guest personally. Tuberculosis took his young mother when he was two, then his foster mother, then his brother. In January 1842, a few months before this story appeared, his wife, Virginia, was singing at the piano when blood came into her mouth. She lingered five years. The Red Death lived among him and his and was not merely the product of fiction.

>>> The Hidden Jewel at Jacksonville State

My mother would have shut the book. She hated stories like these and would not let us celebrate what she considered the devil’s holiday, so my brother and I were costumed in innocence: pirates, Batman and Robin, Superman, a clown, a nerd with tape on his spectacles, Auburn football players in orange and blue.

We could trick-or-treat, but as we grew older, we went instead to youth group for the Reformation Celebration, honoring Luther and his hammer on that same last night of October. Only as a grown man did I understand how my Catholic brethren must see such a party: as a festival of the Church’s broken body, a wound that Protestants and Catholics alike ought to mourn.

Kirk himself crossed that divide, entering the Catholic Church in middle age, and I think he would have seen what Poe’s story finally tells us. Prospero believed walls could save him. Not so long ago, all of us believed it, or were told to. We sealed ourselves in our own abbeys, masked our faces, and watched the clock of the daily COVID death count, while the powerful went on dancing in rooms we were not permitted to enter.

The churches went dark that spring, Catholic and Protestant both, and the old quarrel between them seemed suddenly beside the point. The Mass and the Lord’s Supper were suspended alike; the dying went to God alone, with no priest or pastor at the bedside; and Easter came to empty pews on both sides of the Reformation.

For a season, the divided church was united in the one way none of us would have chosen: in absence. Perhaps that was the lesson. Nothing we bolt shut keeps out the stranger at midnight, and the clock strikes for every room. What the dark cannot touch is what we share. All Hallows’ Eve is only the night before All Saints, and the night of masks gives way, at last, to the morning of faces.

#7645. Setting Guidelines for Using AI in the Classroom

Teachers are doing their best to guide student use of artificial intelligence, but it’s clear that some boundaries are desperately needed.

Stop signs are common. Before the start of this school year, New York City officials banned the use of generative AI for public preschools through eighth grade, and Los Angeles educators banned access to generative AI platforms on school devices for all grade levels.

Parents seem to agree: In recent polls, 75% of them reported supporting pausing AI in schools. But a nearly identical share of respondents (73%) say children already use AI for schoolwork. The technology is here, and let’s face it: Pauses aren’t a long-term solution. Teachers and children need clear guidelines.

AI, after all, is embedded in many online platforms. Alphabet (Google’s parent company) has offered discounted Chromebooks to schools since at least 2011, and Gemini is included in Google’s Chrome web browser. Since Google does not allow its AI summaries or chatbot to be turned off, Fairfax County Public Schools developed its own plug-in to block Google AI search results.

>>> Families and Students Need Guidance on AI

School districts across the country are deciding which forms of AI to ban and for which grade levels, but those choosing to use AI would do well to consider proactive uses of the technology and methods for responsible integration.

State lawmakers must define academic standards and adopt appropriate guardrails for responsible use of AI in classrooms. At its worst, students use AI for companionship in place of friends and to do their homework or write their essays. At its best, students use AI to find, collect, and distill information and identify errors in their own work. AI learning platforms can measure student proficiency in a lesson and build exercises according to their level, following teacher-led instruction.

Even New York City’s restrictions are not banning all forms of AI at the lower grades. City officials allow for the use of programs such as Quill, which helps students with reading comprehension and research and Edia, a math program.

The Heritage Foundation developed model legislation for AI in schools that allows for responsible use of AI in classrooms. The model prioritizes human-centered learning and oversight, transparency, safety and data security. Schools should not be required to adopt AI into lesson plans, but for those that do, educators should help students recognize the difference between getting assistance with homework questions and plagiarism.

State lawmakers should respect parent rights and require schools to obtain parent consent for AI use. Educators should offer parents and students alternatives when families choose to opt out. AI vendors should not gather student data for targeted advertising or sell or rent this information.

Likewise, educators must adhere to state and federal privacy laws such as the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act.

While school officials can allow generative AI programs, teachers should prohibit the use of AI companions that mimic personal relationships. Romantic conversations or simulated friendships do not have academic use and interfere with children’s social skills and healthy development.

>>> The Promise and Peril of Artificial Intelligence in Education  

Florida recently adopted rules for AI in schools that are consistent with many of these provisions. State officials recognize that teachers and students can use AI effectively and banning AI will not eliminate the use of large language models (LLMs) but cause the activity to go unmonitored. If AI use goes underground, the potential for cheating increases, with potentially disastrous consequences for student learning.

Lawmakers should use lessons already available in research and in the media on effective and ineffective uses of technology to advance policy ideas dedicated to protecting student privacy and promoting student learning. Educators can harness the benefits that come from new technologies like AI to help students extend their abilities and not erase them.

State officials should adopt thoughtfully designed boundaries for student and teacher use of AI, including restrictions on non-academic uses of AI. These provisions can allow teachers to blend AI into instructional guidance and help prepare students for the future. AI is part of that future, so let’s use it to our advantage.

#7644. Op-Ed: Crime Drops—Locally Collected Data Drives National Headlines

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

This opinion piece by CJIS Special Agent in Charge Timothy A. Ferguson was published by the Bridgeport News on October 19, 2026.

Across the country, you saw the headlines. Violent crime declined historically last year—dropping an estimated 9.3% from 2024 to 2025. Murder and nonnegligent manslaughter estimated offenses saw an even larger dip of 18.1%.

In West Virginia, crime was also trending downward.

These headlines are based on data reported to the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program by more than 17,000 agencies, covering 96.2% of the U.S. population. It is the responsibility of the FBI’s UCR Program, located within the Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division, in Clarksburg, West Virginia, to collect and publish the data from all 50 states to provide a national picture of reported crime.

This is no small feat. Every day, states and agencies translate local and state crime categories into the national standard and submit their data to the FBI. The UCR Program publishes this data monthly on the Crime Data Explorer to promote transparency and allow you to view timely crime data.

The program also uses the data to develop special reports on topics that matter to you — such as crime in schools, aggravated assault with a firearm, and teen/domestic violence. Then once a year, the program sorts through more than 700 million data points to present you the annual snapshot of crime.

Data collection is just a small fraction of what is accomplished at the CJIS Division. Other efforts also make headlines or prevent you from seeing a tragedy on the news.

Tips actioned by the National Threat Operations Center (NTOC) stop school shootings and help with investigations. Super intelligence capabilities incorporated into NTOC enhance the speed and precision of tip triage, strengthening our ability to process the highest priority tips first so we can promptly share critical threat information with federal, state, and local law enforcement.

Criminal history information from the Interstate Identification Index prevents criminals from becoming your child’s teacher or bus driver. Wants and warrants within the National Crime Information Center help police arrest violent criminals.

Detectives can identify subjects and victims through fingerprints submitted to the Next Generation Identification System.

The division’s mission is to provide our partners with the criminal justice information they need while preserving civil liberties. Sharing that information with officers on the frontlines results in arrests that take criminals off the street and keep neighborhoods safe.

It helps law enforcement return to their families at the end of their shifts. It crushes violent crime and defends the homeland.

When you see headlines of declining crime, know the work to determine that, and the investigations that preceded it, are touched by your neighbors dedicated to the mission at the FBI’s CJIS Division.

Timothy A. Ferguson is assistant director in charge of the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division in Clarksburg, West Virginia. CJIS provides vital systems and services to local, state, tribal, and federal agencies that help ensure public safety. These include the National Crime Information Center; the FBI’s Next Generation Identification System and associated biometric services; the National Instant Criminal Background Check System for firearm purchases; the National Threat Operations Center, which receives and processes tips from the public; and the Uniform Crime Reporting Program, which publishes crime and law enforcement statistical data.

#7642. No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability

Of the many inane comments that socialists have made this year, the one that democracy is “the building block of socialism” might be the most absurd.

Who made the comment? You guessed it: New York City’s boy genius, Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

In a recent episode of “This Past Weekend,” Mr. Mamdani discussed socialism’s ability to ensure affordability with comedian Theo Von. The interview was replete with Marxian nonsense, but Mr. Mamdani also discussed many Americans’ economic frustrations: homeownership feels out of reach; rent is expensive; childcare is unaffordable; and grocery prices are substantially higher.

Young people increasingly feel that the American dream is “slipping away.”

Recognizing affordability problems, however, is not the same as identifying the causes. Mr. Mamdani avers that the free market system cannot solve these problems and that socialism is the silver bullet.

Consider his assertion about democracy. When Mr. Von brought up the concept, Mr. Mamdani interrupted him and claimed, “That’s the building block of socialism.”

>>> Mamdani’s City Grocery Plan Could Leave Taxpayers Paying for Every Banana

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels would like to have a word.

To them, it was clear that implementing socialism—a word that they used interchangeably with communism—would require the opposite of democracy: tyranny.

In their 1848 “The Communist Manifesto,” the owner’s manual for Marxism, Marx and Engels rightly predicted that people would fight back when the government seized their property—something Mr. Mamdani should bear in mind as he upsets more and more New Yorkers with property-grabbing schemes.

“The proletariat will use its political supremacy to wrest, by degrees, all capital from the bourgeoisie, to centralize all instruments of production in the hands of the State,” Marx and Engels wrote. “Of course, in the beginning, this cannot be effected except by means of despotic inroads on the rights of property, and on the conditions of bourgeois production.”

So, no, Mr. Mamdani. Socialism’s pillars are totalitarian, based on forced nationalization and coercive state control.

Now, let us deal with the fanciful claim that socialism is the best way to order society: “Socialism to me means that you have whatever you need to live a dignified life, and it’s the government’s job to deliver on that.”

It sounds compassionate, but what happens when the government assumes responsibility for determining, financing and delivering the necessities of a “dignified life”?

Here, we begin to understand why Mr. Mamdani mixes socialism with democracy. To him, democracy is not just about electing leaders; it is also about letting people choose things that they cannot afford, courtesy of taxpayers.

In line with his big-government agenda, he explained socialism as “the extension of democracy from the ballot box to the rest of your life … your workplace, your home.”

Yet socialists devalue real democracy when they define it as the “right” for people to own what they have not earned. They also devalue the protection of inalienable rights when they insist that 51% of the electorate can suppress individual liberties such as property rights—something America’s Founders called “mobocracy.”

A free society empowers majorities, but it also protects individual rights. More government intervention will neither expand liberty nor make New York City more affordable.

The Big Apple is indeed the most expensive city in the United States and the third most expensive in the world. Mr. Mamdani said that is because “greed is baked into a lot of this economy.” He portrays capitalist profit incentives as a motive for firms to exploit workers, reduce the quality of goods and break the law.

Still, profit and wealth are not social defects to be discouraged; quite the contrary. In competitive markets, signals indicate that entrepreneurs have found ways to provide goods and services that consumers value. These incentives encourage businesses to innovate, produce more, reduce costs and discover better ways to meet people’s needs.

This must be a foreign concept to Mr. Mamdani, who believes that it is the government’s duty to provide the public with everything, from rent to groceries. He ignores commonsense solutions that have worked the world over, such as tax cuts and deregulation—and deportations, for that matter, which would reduce costs for households and businesses alike.

>>> Mamdani Is about to Make Housing Even More Expensive

Instead, Mr. Mamdani turns to central planning, even though government bureaucrats created many of the affordability problems he now insists they will solve.

Take housing. Mr. Mamdani argues that housing costs are central to New York’s economic problems, and many economists agree. Yet the city’s affordability crisis results from decades of restrictive zoning, burdensome permit requirements, development constraints, rent regulation and political barriers that limit housing construction.

The pattern is familiar: Government intervention distorts the market, consumers suffer the consequences, then socialists point to those consequences as evidence of market failure requiring still more state intervention.

Throughout his interview with Mr. Von, Mr. Mamdani framed his socialist ideology as empathetic, not the state-controlled subjugation that it is. Yet remember, the more “necessities” the government promises to provide, the more power bureaucrats require to deliver them.

When the government assumes control over housing, childcare, grocery access, transportation and healthcare, citizens become less self-reliant and more dependent on political institutions.

Americans are right to be concerned about affordability, but the challenge facing them today is how to improve markets with more freedom and opportunity, not socialism.
